summary: Given the head of a doubly linked list, return its values in order as an array.
mainInsight: Nothing clever: follow next pointers from head, appending each value. The prev pointers are irrelevant because you start at the head.

approaches.name: Forward traversal via next
approaches.summary: Walk from head to None appending values.

commonMistakes: Walking prev from the head (returns only the head).
Stopping when node.next is None and missing the last value.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Direct traversal from head following next pointers. Clue: It only asks for the elements of the list in order starting from the given head, so a plain forward walk is all that is needed.
keyPoints: It only asks for the elements of the list in order starting from the given head, so a plain forward walk is all that is needed.
cards.explanation: Recognising that nothing clever is needed is the skill here: the prev pointers are a distraction.

rubric.technique: Direct traversal from head following next pointers

alsoValid.name: Recursively build the list with concatenation
alsoValid.note: correct but concatenation copies the list at each level

rubric.clue: It only asks for the elements of the list in order starting from the given head, so a plain forward walk is all that is needed.

promptVariants: Why are the prev pointers not used?
When would you need prev in this problem?
options: From the head, next alone reaches every node
prev pointers are always None in this input
Using prev would visit the nodes twice
prev only exists on the tail node
cards.answer: From the head, next alone reaches every node
cards.explanation: prev would matter only if you were given an arbitrary node (that is the follow-up variant, Convert Doubly Linked List to Array II).

incorrectOptionExplanations.prev pointers are always None in this in: They are set for every node but the head.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Using prev would visit the nodes twice: From the head, prev just leads to None.
incorrectOptionExplanations.prev only exists on the tail node: Every node has prev; only the head's is None.

promptVariants: What goes wrong with `while node.next: result.append(node.val); node = node.next`?
Which value does a loop on node.next miss?
options: The last node's value is never appended
The head's value is appended twice
It loops forever on a single node
It appends values in reverse order
cards.answer: The last node's value is never appended
cards.explanation: The loop stops at the tail without appending it. Loop while node is not None instead.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The head's value is appended twice: Each visited node is appended once.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It loops forever on a single node: With one node, node.next is None and the loop never runs.

promptVariants: A list with a single node of value 7. What is returned?
head is one node, val 7, prev and next None. Result?
cards.explanation: The loop runs once for the head and stops at None.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[]: The head itself is a node and must be included.
incorrectOptionExplanations.None: The function always returns a list.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time of the traversal.
cards.explanation: One visit and one amortised O(1) append per node.

promptVariants: Besides the returned array, the traversal uses O(___) space.
Auxiliary space excluding the output: O(___).
cards.explanation: Just one pointer; the output array is O(n) and required.
